solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Region of Split (4)

blocks.note: a plain synonym: an area or section of a whole
the verb: to divide or separate, as a crowd or the Red Sea

annotation.surface: A reference to somewhere in or around the Croatian city of Split.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital S makes Split look like the Croatian port; capitals can be ignored, so it is just the verb 'split'.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are plain synonyms: a noun for a section of a whole, and a verb for separating, as lovers or the waves do.

entries.clue: Pole in office turning on Letterman? (10)

indicatorNotes.in: the pole goes inside the rest
indicatorNotes.turning: something turning ends up facing the other way, so 'on' is read backwards

blocks.note: a post is an office or job

annotation.surface: A Polish official in some office, apparently turning on the American talk-show host David Letterman.
annotation.walkthrough: Pole looks like a Polish person and Letterman like the talk-show host; really a pole is a MAST, and a 'letter man' is someone in charge of the letters, i.e. the mail.
annotation.definitionFit: A jokey whole-word reading: the man in charge of the letters at a post office.

entries.clue: Trouble in extremely rambunctious bars (5)

indicatorNotes.in: the trouble sits inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.extremely: take only the extremes, first and last, of 'rambunctious'

blocks.note: the first and last letters of RAMBUNCTIOUS

annotation.surface: Trouble breaking out in some very rowdy pubs.
annotation.walkthrough: Bars look like drinking places to go with the rowdiness, but they are metal bars.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: straight metal or wooden bars, as on a fence or a staircase.

entries.clue: I file release order, maybe (5,5)

annotation.definitionNote: the answer speaks for itself: an emery board would say 'I file'

indicatorNotes.release: the letters of 'order, maybe' are released to rearrange freely

annotation.surface: An official or clerk saying they will file a release order, perhaps for a prisoner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Release order' reads as one legal document, and 'maybe' as a hedge; in fact 'release' is the instruction and 'order, maybe' is the fodder. 'I file' is the answer speaking.
annotation.definitionFit: The answer speaks: an emery board is a nail file, so in its own voice it says 'I file'.

entries.clue: Flash atop front of liner in 1am light show? (7)

indicatorNotes.atop: in a down entry, the first piece sits on top of the second

blocks.note: to moon is to flash one's bare bottom
the bow is the front of a ship

annotation.surface: Someone flashing on the front of a cruise liner during a late-night light show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flash' looks like a burst of light to go with the light show, but it is the rude sense. The question mark flags a playful definition: a rainbow at night.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a rainbow lit by moonlight, so a light show in the small hours.

entries.clue: Start working late as messing about on river? (7)

indicatorNotes.Start: the first letter of the word is the one affected
indicatorNotes.late: late means dead, gone: the start is removed

blocks.note: grafting is British slang for working hard; its first letter is 'late', gone

annotation.surface: Someone starting work late because they were idling about on the river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Late' seems to mean behind time, but here it means deceased: the first letter is gone. Graft is British slang for hard work.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: paddling down a river on a raft is one way of messing about on it.

entries.clue: Beastly type with Dutch Vandyke? (5)

blocks.note: a bear is a type of beast

annotation.surface: A beastly character with the Dutch painter Van Dyck, or Vandyke.
annotation.walkthrough: Vandyke looks like the Flemish painter, but a Vandyke is the pointed style of facial hair seen in his portraits.
annotation.definitionFit: An eponym: the short pointed style worn by men in Van Dyck's portraits is called a Vandyke.

entries.clue: King to stop intermediary visiting a state (9)

indicatorNotes.to stop: the king plugs, or stops, a gap in the intermediary

blocks.note: an agent acts between two parties

annotation.surface: A king trying to stop a go-between from visiting a certain state.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To stop' reads as preventing someone, but it means plugging a hole: the king goes inside the go-between.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a sovereign country in South America.

entries.clue: Awful father making son start to despair (4)

indicatorNotes.making: the son is made into the other letter
indicatorNotes.start to: only the first letter of 'despair' is used

blocks.note: S = son, the letter swapped out
first letter of DESPAIR, swapped in

annotation.surface: A terrible father driving his son to despair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Making son' reads as the father's cruelty to his boy; it is the instruction to turn the S into something else.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: terrible, dreadful, as in dire weather.

entries.clue: World-class fighter who wasn’t well-heeled? (8)

blocks.note: reads as a champion boxer, but means the greatest warrior of the ancient world
reads as 'who wasn't rich', but literally means his heel was not sound: it was his one vulnerable spot

annotation.surface: A top boxer who grew up poor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Well-heeled' means rich, but read literally it means sound in the heel; Achilles, the greatest Greek warrior at Troy, died from an arrow in his heel.
annotation.definitionFit: The Greek champion at Troy, invulnerable except for the heel by which he was dipped in the Styx.

entries.clue: Cot whiffs? To change or to go to sleep? (6,3)

indicatorNotes.To change: the letters of 'cot whiffs' are to change places

annotation.surface: A smelly cot: change the baby, or just let them go to sleep?
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a parent's nappy dilemma; 'To change' is the instruction, not a nappy change.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to stop paying attention, or to drop off to sleep.

entries.clue: Wind up in French town, missing last of stops (5)

indicatorNotes.missing: the town is missing, lacking, the letter named, so it is dropped
indicatorNotes.last of: only the final letter of 'stops' is involved

blocks.note: a town on the Loire in western France, famous for its castle
the final letter of 'stops', which goes missing

annotation.surface: Someone ending up stranded in a French town after missing the final stop.
annotation.walkthrough: The town is Angers. 'Wind up' looks like ending up somewhere, but it is British slang for annoying someone.
annotation.definitionFit: A British idiom: to wind someone up is to provoke or rile them.

entries.clue: Famous player in eatery close to Dubai (5)

blocks.note: the dining hall of a military unit

annotation.surface: A celebrity sportsman spotted in a restaurant near Dubai.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Close to' means the last letter, not nearby; a mess is where soldiers or officers eat.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Argentine footballer, among the greatest of all time.

entries.clue: Brilliant bandaging saves lancer at front (8)

indicatorNotes.saves: the bandaging keeps the letter safe inside it
indicatorNotes.at front: only the front letter of 'lancer' is used

blocks.note: binding a wound is bandaging it

annotation.surface: A brilliant field dressing saves a cavalry lancer at the battlefront.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At front' sounds like the front line, but it just means the first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: excellent, dazzling, as in a blinding goal.

entries.clue: Steal fine lamp and head for the hills (4,6)

annotation.surface: A thief pinches a nice lamp and then runs away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fine' reads as describing the lamp, but it is just its abbreviation F.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for fleeing: running away as a bird escapes into the air.

entries.clue: Everyone in, say, Love Island is superficial (7)

blocks.note: Love Island is an example of a TV show

annotation.surface: A jibe that everyone on the reality programme Love Island is superficial.
annotation.walkthrough: Love Island is a British reality dating programme; 'say' marks it as an example of the word needed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lacking depth, of water or of people.

entries.clue: A line actor put in post for leading man (5,4)

indicatorNotes.put in: the actor is put inside the post

blocks.note: a pale is a fence post or stake
a ham is an overacting actor

annotation.surface: A theatre casting note: an actor with a single line gets posted in as the leading man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leading man' sounds theatrical after 'actor' and 'line', but it means the dominant male of a group.
annotation.definitionFit: Borrowed from animal behaviour: the dominant male of a pack, who leads the rest.

entries.clue: One opens present with a refreshment (7)

indicatorNotes.opens: the one goes into the middle of the present, opening it up

annotation.surface: Someone opening a gift while having a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a gift and a drink; 'opens' means the one goes inside the present, not that it is unwrapped.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: an Italian dessert of coarse flavoured ice, cooling in summer.

entries.clue: Wildly entreat a killer of soldiers? (8)

annotation.surface: A desperate plea to an assassin who has been killing troops.
annotation.walkthrough: Soldiers are soldier ants here, the caste that defends the colony.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: soldier ants guard the colony, and this long-snouted mammal eats them.

entries.clue: Old act with foremost of dancers on show (7)

blocks.note: to pose is to put on an act

annotation.surface: A vintage stage act with the leading dancers on show.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a variety bill; 'act' is a pretence, not a turn on stage.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: uncovered, laid bare for all to see.

entries.clue: Biblical figure revolutionary greeted without zeal ultimately (7)

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: a revolution is a turn, so the greeting is turned round
indicatorNotes.without: in its old sense of outside: the reversed word goes round the letter

annotation.surface: A biblical figure who welcomed a revolutionary with little enthusiasm.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a person being greeted, but it is the instruction; 'without' here means outside, not lacking.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the woman in Judges who betrayed Samson to the Philistines.

entries.clue: Do you despise leaving husband for trip? (7)

annotation.surface: A question: does someone hate the way a husband walks out for a holiday?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trip' reads as a journey, but it is the verb, as in tripping a switch.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical sense: to set a mechanism working, as you trip a switch or a relay.

entries.clue: One did agency work in hearing for trial (7)

indicatorNotes.in hearing: what is heard, not what is written

blocks.note: one (a) temped, worked through an agency

annotation.surface: An agency worker took part in a court hearing ahead of a trial.
annotation.walkthrough: Hearing and trial sound like a courtroom; to temp is to do agency office work.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a try, a go at something.

entries.clue: Good relative allowed one to take knight’s hand (8)

annotation.surface: A kindly aunt permits someone to take a knight's hand, as in marriage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Take a hand' sounds like accepting a proposal, but the answer takes the hand by covering it.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the armoured glove that a knight's hand goes into.

entries.clue: What game is overlooked by New Statesman (5)

indicatorNotes.is overlooked by: in a down entry, the new letter sits on top of, overlooking, the rest

annotation.surface: A question about which sport the New Statesman magazine ignores.
annotation.walkthrough: The New Statesman is a British political weekly, but here 'New' and 'Statesman' come apart.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Jawaharlal, India's first prime minister after independence.

entries.clue: White knight or pawn finally put in a set (5)

indicatorNotes.put in: the letter is put inside the rest

blocks.note: to gel is to set, like jelly

annotation.surface: Chess talk: the white knight or a pawn moved into a set.
annotation.walkthrough: The chess setting is a decoy: a white knight is a rescuer, especially of a company facing takeover.
annotation.definitionFit: Business slang: a backer who rescues a venture or funds a show, just as a white knight saves a company.

entries.clue: Cook right to take breather? Au contraire! (5)

indicatorNotes.to take: one piece takes the other inside it
indicatorNotes.Au contraire!: French for 'on the contrary': swap roles, so the breather takes the right

blocks.note: a fish breathes through its gills

annotation.surface: A chef asking whether they have the right to a breather, and being told no.
annotation.walkthrough: Read straight, R takes in GILL, which fails; 'Au contraire!' reverses the roles.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: cooking under direct overhead heat.

entries.clue: Lump of dope (4)

blocks.note: a thickened mass, as of blood or cream
mild British slang for a fool

annotation.surface: A lump of cannabis resin.
annotation.walkthrough: Dope reads as a drug, but here it is a fool.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a congealed lump, and a British term for an idiot.

entries.clue: Not all ridicule a showy neckline, might I say (5)

indicatorNotes.Not all: only part of the phrase is used

annotation.surface: A fashion comment that a flashy neckline shouldn't be mocked by everyone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Neckline' reads as the cut of a dress; 'might I say' flags a whimsical definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A whimsical definition: the line clipped to a dog's collar is, literally, a neck line.

entries.clue: Sleeping without dreams ultimately is ponderous (9)

indicatorNotes.without: in its plain sense of lacking: the letter is taken away

blocks.note: last letter of DREAMS, the one removed

annotation.surface: Dreamless sleep described as heavy and slow.
annotation.walkthrough: The S lost is at the front of the word, though it comes from the end of 'dreams'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: moving heavily and clumsily.

entries.clue: They send up the Stones set and butcher playing (10)

indicatorNotes.playing: the letters play about into a new order

annotation.surface: Impressionists mocking the Rolling Stones' set and some butchered playing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Send up' looks like parody and 'the Stones' like the band, but the answer means siege engines that hurl stones up and over walls.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: medieval siege engines that hurled stones over castle walls.

entries.clue: Depressed gaining pound, needing to shed pounds? (4)

indicatorNotes.gaining: the word gains a letter inside it

blocks.note: someone who needs to lose pounds is fat

annotation.surface: Feeling low after putting on weight and needing to lose it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pound' in the singular is the letter L; 'pounds' at the end is the weight, pointing to the host word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: low in spirits, lifeless.
